lines.text: Viking traders, warrior kings, a Baltic empire, and then two centuries of peace. This is the story of Sweden, from Birka to NATO.
It begins with the Vikings. On an island in Lake Malaren, Birka grew into a busy trading town, linking the north with lands far to the east.
By the end of the tenth century, Christian kings were drawing the Swedes together into one kingdom.
Where Lake Malaren meets the Baltic, Stockholm rose on its islands, a city that would become the capital.
In 1397 Sweden joined Denmark and Norway under one crown in the Kalmar Union, an uneasy partnership.
Gustav Vasa was born, the noble who would one day free Sweden from that union.
In 1520 the Danish king had some eighty Swedish nobles killed in Stockholm. The Bloodbath set off a war for independence.
Gustav Vasa won, and became king in 1523. His grandson Gustavus Adolphus would reform the army and lead Sweden into the Thirty Years War, dying in battle at Lutzen.
Under him Sweden became a great power, ruling lands all around the Baltic for more than a century.
Its pride was the warship Vasa, which sank minutes into her first voyage because she was top heavy. Raised in 1961, she now fills a museum.
Carl Linnaeus was born, the naturalist who would give every living thing a two-part Latin name, a system still used today.
Two years later, at Poltava, Peter the Great crushed the army of Charles the Twelfth, and Sweden's age as a great power began to end.
Sweden turned to trade. Ships of the East India Company sailed from Gothenburg to Canton for tea, porcelain and silk.
Alfred Nobel was born in Stockholm. He invented dynamite, and left his fortune to fund prizes for the good of humanity.
In 1901 the first Nobel Prizes were given, in physics, chemistry, medicine, literature and peace.
Dag Hammarskjold was born. He would lead the United Nations, build up its peacekeeping, and die in a plane crash on a peace mission.
That same year came Greta Garbo, who would become one of Hollywood's great stars, then retire at thirty-five.
Astrid Lindgren was born, who would write Pippi Longstocking and delight children everywhere.
In 1912 Stockholm hosted the Olympic Games, with electric timing and athletes from all five inhabited continents.
Ingmar Bergman was born, the director whose films, like The Seventh Seal, would wrestle with faith and death.
In 1927 the first Volvo cars rolled out in Gothenburg, and the name became a byword for safety.
In the middle of the Second World War, which neutral Sweden stayed out of, Ingvar Kamprad founded IKEA, later famous for its flat-pack furniture.
In 1958 Sweden hosted the football World Cup, where a seventeen-year-old Pele helped Brazil to its first title.
In 1972 four young Swedes formed ABBA. Two years later they won Eurovision with Waterloo, and conquered the world's charts.
The ferry Estonia entered service. In 1994 it sank in a Baltic storm on its way to Stockholm, with the loss of hundreds of lives.
In 1986 Prime Minister Olof Palme was shot dead on a Stockholm street, a shock to a peaceful country.
Greta Thunberg was born. Her school strike for the climate in 2018 would start a worldwide youth movement.
That same year, The Pirate Bay went online, a file-sharing site that courts could never quite shut down.
Then Spotify launched from Stockholm, and streaming changed how the whole world listens to music.
And in 2024, after more than two centuries without war or alliance, Sweden ended its neutrality and joined NATO.
From Viking longships to streaming music, Sweden keeps finding new ways to reach the world.
